newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus holds Soviet-style independence parade.
newsitem.headline: Belarus holds Soviet-style independence parade.

text.p: Belarus stepped back in time on Thursday, staging a highly militarised, Soviet-style parade to mark the republic's liberation from fascism.

Military jets flew over Independence Square, where hardline President Alexander Lukashenko stood with top officials by the government building to review a parade of tanks and military equipment not seen since the days of the Soviet Union.

The troops were followed by athletes turning somersaults, playing tennis on the move and doing gymnastics in front of the presidential podium in scenes reminiscent of the era of Soviet dictator Josef Stalin.

Admission to the square, where around 5,000 people gathered with red flags and portraits of Lukashenko, was restricted to those with special passes. Others were kept away by lines of police and soldiers.

"For every citizen of our country this date has a special significance -- our people, who have lived through the suffering of the fascist onslaught and known the joy of great victory, July 3 is a symbol of true independence," said Lukashenko.
Until last November, Independence Day was celebrated in Belarus on July 27, the date in 1991 when Belarus declared limited sovereignty in the former Soviet Union.
It was moved after a controversial referendum to July 3, the anniversary of Minsk's liberation from Nazi occupation in 1944.
Belarus, where one in four people died during World War Two, suffered hugely from the occupation. Nazi troops burned whole villages with their inhabitants and set up concentration camps.
Last year's referendum, criticised by international human rights groups, was initiated by Lukashenko, who used it to crack down on the opposition and increase his powers.
Lukashenko has played on widespread nostalgia for the Soviet Union and concluded an integration deal with Russia this year which his opponents said signed away Belarussian independence.

"After the war Belarus managed not only to revive its economy but created a powerful state...We will carry out our own independent policy in the interests of our people," the moustachioed leader said from a specially-constructed podium.

"However such an approach does not suit those who have got rich on separatism and nationalism. Today they are playing a new card, trying to present Belarus as a totalitarian state," he said, in front of a statue of Bolshevik leader Vladimir Lenin.
The parade, held on a drizzly day, kicked off three days of concerts, plays and fireworks, contrasting with the modest meetings and opposition rallies of previous Independence Days.
Opposition parties criticised Lukashenko for spending more on the festivities than on disaster relief after a fierce storm last week killed four people, injured 50 and left many homeless.
The Belarussian parliament appealed to foreign governments and international organisations for aid. But Lukashenko said that everyone who had suffered had received state help.

Many World War Two veterans and elderly people were among the crowd on the square and some cried when they saw soldiers wearing the old uniforms in the first row of the parade, which began with the scream of military jets overhead.
"We need such parades, to pay our debt of memory to the generation which lived through the war," said 79-year-old Ivan Byako, who said he had voted for the change in the plebiscite.

"For the first time in six years we have repeated something good from the Soviet Union -- a mighty military parade," said Viktor Voltsetsky, a 49-year-old builder. "I would like to return to the USSR, but without a dictatorship," he said.

"Who is this parade for? They didn't even let us onto the square," said Yuri Belyakin, 24. "There's nothing for us to celebrate, because Belarus is not independent. We live worse than ever. Today's parade is like dancing at a funeral."
